about: CSV Studio converts tabular data between CSV, JSON, XML and TOON, and lets you query it with JSONPath. Every conversion goes through the same intermediate shape, an array of flat records, so any input format can be written out as any other. You paste text or drop a file, pick the input and output formats, and the converted result appears next to a preview table.

The practical uses are the usual ones. A spreadsheet export needs to become JSON for an API call, a JSON array from a service needs to open in Excel, or a config feed arrives as XML and you want rows. The query mode adds a fifth job: filter or project the rows with an RFC 9535 JSONPath expression and export the matches as JSON or CSV.

Parsing, conversion and queries happen in the page. The README states there is no backend and no arbitrary network calls, and that file contents are processed only in the browser. Copy and download go through the host's permission broker, and a declined permission leaves the output in the editor for manual copying.

CSV is rectangular text with no types and no nesting, so the tool is explicit about what it will and will not do. It rejects ragged rows, duplicate headers and nested XML instead of guessing. If your data is nested JSON that needs inspection first, start in [JSON Tools](/json-tools/); to turn records into typed classes afterwards, use [POJO to Any](/pojo-to-any/).

features.title: Four formats, any direction
features.body: CSV, JSON, XML and TOON are all readable and writable. The XML dialect is a fixed `<rows><row><field name="...">` layout, and TOON uses the official `@toon-format/toon` encoder and decoder.

features.title: Separator auto-detection
features.body: Leave Separator on Auto-detect or force comma, tab, semicolon or pipe. Importing a file with a `.tsv` extension sets tab automatically. Quoted fields, doubled quotes and multiline cells are handled by the PapaParse library.

features.title: Optional type inference
features.body: Values stay strings unless you enable inference. With it on, `true`, `false` and `null` become JSON literals and plain decimal numbers become numbers. Values with a leading zero, hex, exponent notation or unsafe integers stay strings.

features.title: Spreadsheet-safe CSV output
features.body: The Excel-safe option escapes cells that start with formula characters such as `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` so that opening the file in a spreadsheet cannot execute a formula. It is on by default and uses CRLF line endings.

features.title: JSONPath query mode
features.body: Run an RFC 9535 expression over the records at `$`, for example `$[*].name` or `$[?@.price > 100]`. Results can be shown as JSON or exported as CSV, with scalar results wrapped as `{value: ...}` rows.

features.title: Preview and bounds
features.body: A preview table shows at most eight rows and eight columns. Hard limits are 2 MiB of input, 20,000 records, 120 columns and 12 MiB of output.

reference.title: Format rules, type inference and the XML and TOON shapes

head: Input format
Accepted shape
Rejected with an error
rows: First row is headers; every later row has the same field count
Blank or duplicate headers, `__proto__`, `prototype` and `constructor` headers, rows with the wrong number of fields
Array of objects, or an object with exactly one array property
Scalars, arrays of arrays, objects with zero or several array properties
Other roots, nested elements inside a field, duplicate field names, DOCTYPE or ENTITY declarations
Decodes to the same shapes as JSON, parsed in strict mode
Anything TOON can express that CSV cannot, such as a bare scalar root

blocks.text: Row errors name the row. A ragged CSV reports something like `Row 4 has 3 fields, expected 5`, with the number counting the header as row 1. Skipping blank lines is automatic, and a leading byte-order mark is stripped before parsing.

CSV has no types, so the tool defaults to the safe choice and keeps every field as a string. That preserves ZIP codes, phone numbers and identifiers exactly. When you turn inference on, only the following are converted.
Use the same inference setting when comparing numbers in a query. A filter like `$[?@.price > 100]` compares numerically only if `price` was converted to a number, while strings compare lexically.

Converting JSON with nested objects or arrays to CSV stores each such cell as JSON text, for example `{"city":"Oslo"}`. It does not flatten into dotted columns, and converting that CSV back leaves the cell as a string. Keys are collected across all records, so records with different fields still produce one rectangular table with empty cells for missing values.

The importer also accepts simple child elements such as `<name>Ana</name>` directly under `<row>`. TOON (Token-Oriented Object Notation) is a compact text format aimed at feeding structured data to language models. For arrays of uniform objects it writes a header with the field names once and then one line per row, which is why CSV-like data converts into it naturally. Compare the result with the JSON form using [Diff Checker](/diff-checker/) if you need to confirm nothing was lost.

example.title: Filter a product export and hand it to a spreadsheet user

blocks.text: Start with this semicolon-separated export, as produced by many European spreadsheet locales.

items: Paste it with input format CSV and Separator on Auto-detect. The preview shows three rows and three columns.
Turn on type inference. Convert to JSON and check that `price` is a number while `sku` is still `"00123"`, because the leading zero blocks conversion.
Switch to query mode and enter `$[?@.price > 100]`. Two matches come back: Desk lamp and Chair.
Set Query result as CSV and copy the output. The Excel-safe option is on, so a name like `=SUM(A1)` would be prefixed to stay text.

blocks.text: Result: a two-row comma-separated CSV with CRLF line endings that opens correctly in a spreadsheet, produced without editing the original file.

limits: Only flat records are supported. Nested JSON survives as embedded JSON text in a cell, and nested XML is rejected rather than flattened.
Hard limits: 2 MiB input, 20,000 records, 120 columns and 12 MiB output. For larger files use a command-line tool such as `mlr` or `xsv`, or split the file.
The XML dialect is fixed to `<rows><row>`. Arbitrary XML documents, attributes and namespaces are not mapped to columns. For general XML to JSON conversion use [JSON Tools](/json-tools/).
Character encoding is UTF-8. Files saved in legacy encodings such as Windows-1252 may show replacement characters and should be re-saved as UTF-8 first.
There is no sorting, deduplication, joins or column renaming. The tool converts and filters, it is not a spreadsheet.

faq.question: Why did my CSV fail with a field count error?
faq.answer: Every data row must have the same number of fields as the header. A common cause is an unquoted comma inside a value. Wrap such values in double quotes and double any quote inside them.

faq.question: Why are my numbers still quoted in the JSON?
faq.answer: Type inference is off by default so identifiers are not corrupted. Enable it to convert plain numbers, booleans and null. Values such as `007` are deliberately kept as strings.

faq.question: What does the Excel-safe option do?
faq.answer: Spreadsheet programs can execute cells that begin with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` as formulas, which is a known CSV injection risk. The option adds a prefix so those cells are treated as text.

faq.question: Can I convert nested JSON to CSV?
faq.answer: Yes, but nested objects and arrays are written into the cell as JSON text. They are not expanded into extra columns.

faq.question: Is my data sent to a server?
faq.answer: No. Parsing, conversion and queries run in your browser. Copy and download happen only when you ask for them, through the host's permission prompts.

faq.question: Which JSONPath syntax is supported?
faq.answer: RFC 9535 syntax through the `jsonpath-rfc9535` library, including filters like `$[?@.price > 100]`. Queries are limited to 600 characters and 20,000 matches.
